Course 04

Personality without labels

Traits, differences and assessment.

Lesson 3. Labels and myths

1 · Lesson

Personality classifications into four, nine or sixteen "types" are very popular. The problem is that they turn continuous dimensions into boxes: two almost identical people can fall into different types, and the same person can change type if they retake the test weeks later. That is why research prefers to measure dimensions.

Another common error is the Barnum effect (or Forer effect): we tend to accept as very accurate vague descriptions that apply to almost everyone ("sometimes you are sociable and other times you prefer to be alone"). It explains the success of horoscopes and many online tests.

Labels can be useful for conversation, but they carry risks: they can pigeonhole ("that's how I am, I can't change"), justify behaviour or lead others to treat us according to the label rather than what we do.

2 · Example

In 1948, Bertram Forer gave his students a supposedly personalised profile based on a test. In fact, they all received the same text, partly taken from an astrology book. On average, they rated its accuracy above 4 out of 5.

3 · Activity

Find an online personality test and read your result. Underline the sentences that would apply to almost anyone. What is left when you remove them?
